title: Aeroflot 5003 (1977)
summary: Aeroflot Flight 5003, an Ilyushin Il-18V carrying 98 people, crashed near Mineralnye Vody on February 15, 1977 while attempting a go-around after a missed approach. Weather included low-level clouds and fog with visibility 1020-1180 meters. The crew drifted off course during approach, realized the deviation at 1.5 kilometers from the airport, and attempted to abort the landing. During the go-around climb at low altitude, the crew pulled the nose up to 11 degrees, causing a 1.64 G overload that damaged control surfaces. The aircraft entered a steep bank and struck the ground.
probable_cause: During a missed approach go-around in low visibility, the pilot in command pulled the nose up to an excessive angle of attack, causing control surface damage and loss of control.

factors.evidence: Weather conditions at Mineralnye Vody were low-level clouds and fog less than 100 meters above ground with visibility between 1020 and 1180 meters.
Aircraft drifted slightly off course during approach; pilots did not notice until 1.5 kilometers from airport, then changed heading.
Pilot in command pulled nose up to 11 degrees pitch angle during low-altitude go-around, creating 1.64 G overload that damaged control surfaces.
Aircraft experienced stall condition when control surfaces were damaged by excessive G-load maneuver during go-around.
Aircraft entered right bank and continued turning right despite crew attempts to adjust ailerons; flew toward ground.
Aircraft hit ground at 23:17:44 at altitude of 120-130 meters while in left bank, damaging railroad at impact site.

events.text: Aircraft approached Mineralnye Vody Airport at heading of 117 degrees; crew lowered flaps and reduced speed from 290 to 260 km/h while monitoring instruments and searching for landmarks.
At 1.5 kilometers from airport, pilots realized landing deviation and changed heading to 127 degrees; pilot in command realized landing was impossible and initiated go-around for second approach.
During go-around, aircraft did not climb 300 meters in straight line but turned right at 80-90 meters altitude, losing altitude in 4-5 degree roll to 270 km/h.

At altitude of 120-130 meters crew adjusted flaps too quickly; pilot pulled nose up 11 degrees causing 1.64 G overload that damaged ailerons and rudder; aircraft continued turning right and struck ground.

notes: investigation definitively attributed to crew error
sequence of errors in low-visibility conditions documented

title: Tenerife airport disaster
summary: Two Boeing 747s, KLM Flight 4805 and Pan Am Flight 1736, collided on the single runway at Los Rodeos Airport, Tenerife, on 27 March 1977, killing 583 in the deadliest accident in aviation history. Both aircraft had been diverted there after a bomb at their destination, Gran Canaria, and congestion forced departing aircraft to backtaxi along the runway. In dense fog, the KLM captain began his takeoff run believing ATC had cleared him and that the Pan Am jet, still on the runway, had vacated it.
probable_cause: Spanish investigators found the primary cause was the KLM captain's decision to take off believing ATC had issued clearance and that Pan Am had cleared the runway, despite Pan Am radioing it would report when clear; Dutch investigators emphasized a mutual misunderstanding in the radio communications between the KLM crew and ATC.

factors.evidence: Los Rodeos had become congested with parked planes blocking the only taxiway, forcing departing aircraft to taxi on the runway
patches of thick fog were drifting across the airfield, so visibility was greatly reduced
a mutual misunderstanding in radio communications between the KLM crew and ATC
two Boeing 747 passenger jets collided on a runway at Los Rodeos Airport

events.text: A bomb planted by the Canary Islands Independence Movement exploded at Gran Canaria Airport, so both flights were diverted to the smaller Los Rodeos Airport.
Parked aircraft diverted from Gran Canaria blocked the only taxiway at Los Rodeos, forcing the Pan Am 747 to backtaxi along the runway itself.
At 17:06 GMT, in dense fog, the KLM crew began their takeoff run believing air traffic control had issued clearance and that the Pan Am 747 had cleared the runway.
The Pan Am crew had radioed that they would report when clear of the runway, but were still on it when the KLM jet began its takeoff roll.
The KLM 747 collided with the right side of the Pan Am aircraft; the impact and fire killed all 248 aboard the KLM plane and 335 of 396 aboard the Pan Am plane.

notes: two flights involved, no single flight_number
agency left UNKNOWN; text names only 'Spanish authorities' and 'Dutch investigators', no formal board name

title: Southern Airways 242
summary: Southern Airways Flight 242 suffered total loss of thrust from both engines while descending through a severe thunderstorm with embedded cells. The crew had been advised of severe weather but proceeded based on radar display interpretation that was misleading due to radar attenuation of the storm's peak convective activity. The aircraft encountered a massive amount of rain and hail that broke the windshield and caused both engines to ingest water and hail, resulting in compressor stalling and flameout. The crew successfully glided the aircraft unpowered to a forced landing on Georgia State Route 381.
probable_cause: Total loss of thrust from both engines caused by ingestion of massive amounts of water and hail during penetration of severe thunderstorm cell, in combination with thrust lever movement that induced severe stalling and major damage to the engine compressors. The crew's misinterpretation of weather radar attenuation contributed to the decision to penetrate the storm.

factors.evidence: aircraft descended from cruising altitude of 17,000 to near Rome VOR, it apparently entered a thunderstorm cell and encountered a massive amount of rain and hail
The hail was so intense that it broke the aircraft's windshield
they were apparently misled by the radar's attenuation effect, and they proceeded toward what they believed was a low-intensity area, when in fact it was the peak convective activity point
The Pratt & Whitney JT8D-7A engines ingested a massive amount of water and hail causing major damage to the compressors and flameout
The crew attempted unsuccessfully to restart the engines, gliding down unpowered, executing a forced landing on Georgia State Route 381

events.text: Flight cleared to proceed to Rome VOR where peak convective activity was occurring
Aircraft encountered severe thunderstorm with massive rain and hail
Windshield broken by hail; both engines ingested water and hail causing compressor damage and flameout
Crew executed successful forced landing on Georgia State Route 381 in unpowered glide

title: Japan Airlines 715
summary: Japan Air Lines Flight 715, a McDonnell Douglas DC-8-62H, was on approach to Subang Airport in Malaysia on September 27, 1977. The aircraft descended below the minimum descent altitude of 750 feet without having the runway in sight due to poor weather conditions and low clouds. The crew continued descending in instrument meteorological conditions until the aircraft struck a hill near the Elmina Estate, 4 miles from the airport. Of the 79 occupants, 34 were killed and 45 survived with injuries. The investigation determined that the captain violated regulations by descending below minimums without required visual references, and the first officer failed to challenge this violation.
probable_cause: The captain descended below the minimum descent altitude without having the runway in sight, and continued the descent in poor weather conditions with low clouds, causing the aircraft to crash before reaching the airport. The first officer did not challenge the captain for violating regulations.

factors.evidence: The weather around the airport was poor and the aircraft was on a VOR approach with bad weather.
The aircraft descended below minimum descent altitude of 750 ft and crashed into the side of a hill at 300 ft without having the runway in sight.
The first officer did not challenge the captain for violating the regulations regarding descent below minimums.
The aircraft struck the side of a hill 4 miles from the airport near Elmina Estate.

events.text: ATC at Subang Airport instructed flight 715 to start its approach and land on runway 15.
Crew put landing gear down and extended flaps, beginning descent on VOR approach.
Aircraft descended below minimum descent altitude of 750 feet without having the runway in sight.
At 300 feet altitude, aircraft crashed into the side of a hill 4 miles from the airport near Elmina Estate.

title: TAP Portugal 425
summary: The aircraft was on approach to Madeira in poor visibility caused by severe weather with thunderstorm cumulus and rain. After two unsuccessful approaches with no visual contact with the runway, the crew made a final landing at excessive speed (148 knots, 19 knots above recommended) and touched down 2060 feet from the runway beginning, 1060 feet farther than normal. Aquaplaning on the wet runway led to a runway overrun and crash onto the nearby beach.
probable_cause: The flight crew violated the approach procedure, resulting in the aircraft touching down far down the runway at excessive speed. Difficult weather conditions, aquaplaning on the runway, and the overshoot landing speed of 19 knots were immediate causes.

factors.evidence: At 9:23:13 the crew reported no visual contact with the ground, and at 9:26:33 the crew reported no visual contact with the runway
According to the forecast, severe weather was expected en route, with a chance of thunderstorm cumulus and torrential rain
The crew descended toward the runway with no visual contact and initiated a go-around at 1,700 feet
The flight crew violated the approach procedure
The aircraft touching down 2060 ft from the beginning of the runway
The speed was 148.2 kn, which is 19.2 kn above the recommended speed
Aquaplaning on the runway was noted as an immediate cause
The aircraft overran the airport's runway before crashing onto the nearby beach

events.text: Flight 425 descended toward Madeira in poor weather and visibility conditions.
The crew requested permission to descend to flight level 50
The crew contacted air traffic control in Funchal and was cleared to descend to 3,500 feet on QNH 1013 for landing on runway 06
The crew reported passing the MAD beacon at 1,700 feet but had no visual contact with the ground
Flight TP425 reported no visual contact with the runway and initiated a go-around
After two unsuccessful attempts to land, the aircraft made a final approach, touching down 2060 feet from the runway beginning at 148.2 knots
The aircraft overran the runway and crashed onto the nearby beach, exploding

title: 1977 Benghazi Libyan Arab Airlines Tu-154 crash
summary: A Tu-154A leased from Balkan Bulgarian Airlines carrying 159 hajj pilgrims and 6 crew took off from Jiddah for Benghazi. Egyptian airspace was closed to Libyan aircraft, requiring an indirect route that was longer than planned. The crew did not plan for the longer flight time, leaving the aircraft short of fuel. Heavy fog blanketed Benghazi airport, preventing landing. After failing to locate the alternate airport, the aircraft ran out of fuel and made a forced landing, killing 59 occupants.
probable_cause: Fuel exhaustion due to crew failure to plan for indirect routing and inadequate fuel reserves when Egyptian airspace was closed to Libyan aircraft.

factors.evidence: the crew reportedly did not plan for the longer flight time, leaving the aircraft short of fuel
heavy fog blanketed the airport and the pilots could not land the aircraft
After failing to locate the alternate airport, the aircraft ran out of fuel
the aircraft ran out of fuel and made a forced landing, killing 59 out of the 165 on board

events.text: Aircraft took off from Jiddah International Airport with 159 pilgrims and 6 crew for flight to Benghazi
As aircraft neared Benghazi, heavy fog blanketed the airport and pilots could not land the aircraft
After failing to locate the alternate airport, aircraft encountered fuel exhaustion situation
Made forced landing in Libya killing 59 of 165 on board after running out of fuel

notes: Egyptian airspace closure requiring indirect route is documented; crew planning failure with fuel calculations inferred from text

title: Malaysian Airline System 653
summary: Malaysian Airline System Flight 653 was hijacked as it descended toward Kuala Lumpur on 4 December 1977. Someone knocked on the cockpit door and one or more hijackers suddenly barged into the cockpit. The pilots were forced to cut off all communications. Investigators heard a series of gunshots on the cockpit voice recorder and concluded that both pilots were fatally shot, leaving the aircraft professionally uncontrolled until it impacted the ground at near-vertical angle at Tanjung Kupang, killing all 100 people aboard.
probable_cause: The aircraft was hijacked by person or persons unknown. Investigators concluded the hijackers incapacitated both pilots through fatal gunshots, resulting in uncontrolled descent and impact with the ground.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was hijacked by person or persons unknown.
Investigators concluded that both the pilot and co-pilot were fatally shot by the hijacker.
The pilots were forced to cut off all communications by one or more hijackers who suddenly barged into the cockpit.
The aircraft's trajectory became unrecoverable, resulting in its impact with the ground at a near-vertical angle at very high speed.

events.text: Someone knocked on the cockpit door and one or more hijackers suddenly barged into the cockpit.
The crew reported to Subang Tower that an unidentified hijacker was on board, and the tower immediately notified the authorities.
The crew radioed they were proceeding to Singapore, followed by a series of gunshots on the cockpit voice recorder.
The aircraft hit the ground at a near-vertical angle at very high speed, and there were no survivors.
